newsitem.title: USA: Midwest Grain sees return to profit in Q2.
newsitem.headline: Midwest Grain sees return to profit in Q2.

text.p: Midwest Grain Products Inc, a grain processor, said Thursday it expects to report a profit in the fiscal second quarter.
Earlier, it reported a loss for the first quarter ended September 30 of $0.04 a share, compared with a year-ago loss of $0.24 a share.

The company said its operating income was positive in the first quarter. "This is consistent with strengthened conditions in the marketplace, which indicate a return to profitability in the second quarter," Ladd Seaberg, president, said in a statement.

Prices for corn and sorghum, which Midwest Grain uses in its alcohol production, averaged 54 percent more per bushel. Prices for wheat, which the company mills into flour and then further processes into wheat gluten and premium wheat starch, averaged seven percent more per bushel compared to prices paid in the first quarter of fiscal 1996.

The combination of higher grain costs and relatively flat prices for wheat gluten and fuel alcohol early in the first quarter prompted the decision to extend a maintenance and repair shutdown at the Pekin, Ill., plant through the first half of July, Midwest Grain said.

"Although production levels declined as the result of this shutdown, the decision allowed us to minimize the negative impact of the exceptionally high grain costs," Seaberg said. "Furthermore, as the quarter progressed, demand for our fuel alcohol as well as our food grade alcohol for beverage and industrial applications strengthened."

Conditions in the company's alcohol markets remain favorable, and corn and sorghum prices have dropped from their July record levels. Conditions in wheat gluten, however, continue to be severely affected by the growing presence of gluten imports from the European Union, Seaberg said.

"Consultations between the United States and (European Union), which are expected to help level the playing field, have not yet been completed as we previously had hoped," he said. "In the meantime, possibilities for a remedy through legal action are being aggressively explored."

The company said it is accelerating the development of non-commodity specialty wheat gluten products for both food and industrial applications. The growth of these products, however, is expected to be gradual.
